# gof

**Model diagnostics based on cumulative residuals.**

`gof` checks fitted mean relationships by accumulating residuals along a
covariate or the fitted predictions. It compares the observed curve with
simulated null curves and reports Sup and L2 test p-values. This can help
identify a missing nonlinear term or another systematic pattern that a
coefficient table does not describe.

The package provides methods for `lm`, Gaussian/binomial/Poisson `glm`,
Gaussian structural equation models fitted with `lava`, and `lava` ordinal
regression. It also has an interface for supplied residuals, gradients and
coefficient influences. Each method has explicit assumptions and support
limits in its help page.

## A complete diagnostic workflow

This example deliberately fits a straight line to a curved relationship.
The random seed makes the data and Monte Carlo calculation reproducible.

```{r example}
library(gof)

set.seed(42)
d <- data.frame(x = seq(-2, 2, length.out = 200))
d$y <- 1 + 0.5 * d$x + 0.7 * d$x^2 + rnorm(nrow(d))

diagnostic <- lm(y ~ x, data = d) |>
  cumres(variable = "x", R = 499, plots = 25)

diagnostic |> as.data.frame()
```

```{r diagnostic-plot, fig.alt="Observed cumulative residual curve compared with 25 simulated null curves along x; the curved mean omitted from the fitted model produces a systematic residual pattern."}
diagnostic |> plot(idx = "x", legend = "type2")
```

A small p-value indicates that this aspect of the fitted model deserves
attention. A large p-value does not establish that the model is correct.
Sup and L2 summarize the same residual process in different ways. The
p-values are Monte Carlo estimates; a reported zero means none of the
simulated statistics reached the observed value, rather than an exact
probability of zero. Increase `R` when more simulation precision is needed.

The base-R table contains explicit `variable`, `test`, `statistic`,
`p.value`, `n`, `nobs`, `R`, `informative` and `aggregation` columns. No tidyverse package is
needed for native `|>` pipelines. Optional `broom::tidy(diagnostic)` or
`generics::tidy(diagnostic)` returns the same columns as a tibble when the
corresponding optional packages are installed. Existing `coef(diagnostic)`
calls retain their historical wide p-value table.

## Installation

This is a local maintenance snapshot of Klaus K. Holst's
[original gof project](https://github.com/kkholst/gof). The changes in this
checkout have not been published to CRAN or the upstream repository.
Installing the upstream version does not install these repairs.

To install a supplied source archive, first install its runtime and compiler
interface dependencies, then install that archive:

```{r install-archive, eval=FALSE}
install.packages(c("lava", "Rcpp", "RcppArmadillo", "numDeriv", "lpSolve"))
install.packages("gof_1.2.0.tar.gz", repos = NULL, type = "source")
```

From the root of a checkout, this also builds the installed guides:

```{r install-checkout, eval=FALSE}
install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_local(".", dependencies = TRUE, build_vignettes = TRUE)
```

R 4.1 or later and a C++17 toolchain are required. Source installation needs
the development tools appropriate to your R installation; Windows users
need the matching Rtools, and macOS users need the command-line developer
tools. C++23 is a separately tested integration configuration, ahead of the
planned native-code modernization.

## Help and worked guides

The same function reference is available in RStudio's Help pane and other
R interfaces:

```{r help, eval=FALSE}
?gof
?cumres
?cumres.glm
?cumres.lvmfit
?cumres.ordreg
?cumres_joint
?cumres_normality
?cumres_bootstrap
?`cumres-object`

vignette("getting-started", package = "gof")
vignette("statistical-details", package = "gof")
vignette("joint-normality-bootstrap", package = "gof")
```

The ordinal default combines the joint cutpoint process for one ordering;
`aggregate="score"` retains the older category-score-mean check, and
`aggregate="cutpoints"` exposes signed components. Mean-preserving changes
in category probabilities can be missed by the score sum.

The guides cover weighted and grouped responses, offsets, missing rows,
moving windows, reproducibility and the assumptions behind custom models.

`subset.max = 500` limits the number of distinct **evaluation points** in
the default/linear/GLM/SEM process. It does not reduce the fitted sample to
500 observations. Tied observations enter the process together. Use
`subset.max = Inf` for every distinct value; ordinal diagnostics use their
own full distinct-value grid. Moving-window grids include entry and exit
events over the complete window support; a finite cap approximates that
full-domain statistic.

## Scope of inference

The implemented multiplier process assumes independent residual units and
a valid coefficient influence representation. Normal/Poisson weights
describe response-mean precision; binomial weights must define integer
trial counts. The SEM method requires complete independent-subject
Gaussian fits; clustered, weighted and incomplete-data SEMs are rejected.
The ordinal method rejects fitting options that the upstream fitter ignores.
Arbitrary callback or ordering functions require a statistical justification
from the caller, including the stronger conditions for estimated orderings.
Numerical convergence alone does not establish a regular interior mean fit;
separation, recession and numerical local-root checks reject unqualified GLMs.
Ordinal score constraints are checked as well.

Recognized zero-information linear/GLM processes are marked
`informative = FALSE`. Numerically unresolved score-space cases have missing
p-values and retain their curves for inspection. An unavailable information
flag in another adapter is distinct from that numerical case; see
`?"cumres-object"`.

The default `cumres()` call provides separate checks for each ordering.
Its saved null curves from different orderings cannot be combined as a
joint draw. `cumres_joint()` instead shares multipliers by subject and
provides family tests and simultaneous null reference envelopes over the
chosen orderings and evaluated grids. This does not check every possible
model departure.

`cumres_normality()` checks Gaussian SEM residual distributions with an
explicit correction for estimated nuisance parameters. It complements
the existing SEM mean/linearity diagnostics. A projected latent-residual
check cannot uniquely identify the source of nonnormality under alternatives.
Its one-step calibration is asymptotic; finite-sample rejection rates can
depart from the nominal level.

The multiplier approximation can fail with rare events, severe imbalance
or little effective information despite a large nominal sample.
`cumres_bootstrap()` supplies model-based calibration for canonical binomial
and Poisson diagnostics. A fitted-null bootstrap remains an approximation;
simulation under genuinely specified means permits a distinct Monte Carlo
test. Failed refits are accounted for rather than silently discarded.
See `vignette("joint-normality-bootstrap", package = "gof")` for supported
models and interpretation.

Regression tests, independent numerical references, calibration experiments
and native sanitizers support the recorded implementation checks. They do
not establish correctness for every supplied model or finite sample.

## Citation and development

Use `citation("gof")` for the software and the Lin, Wei and Ying (2002)
method reference. The original authorship and license are retained. The
SEM help page also cites the relevant structural-model method paper.

`NEWS.md` records user-visible changes. `DEVELOPMENT.md` explains reproducible
documentation and package checks; `CONTRIBUTING.md` describes how to report
or propose a change. The repository audit records distinguish statistical
support boundaries, passed local checks and platform jobs still to run.

The documentation site can be built locally with
`pkgdown::build_site(preview = FALSE)`. Building it does not publish it.
